message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • The landlord may hold a maximum of **one month’s rent** (or two if the lease is for a month‑to‑month tenancy).
• The deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any move‑in inspection report.
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • The landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control).
• Repairs must be made within a **reasonable time** after you notify the landlord. | • Notify the landlord in writing (email or certified mail) and keep a copy.
• If repairs are not made, you may withhold rent, repair and deduct, or file a complaint with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA). | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are **reasonable** (no more than 5% of the monthly rent). | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Lease Termination** | • **Month‑to‑month**: Either party may terminate with **30 days’ written notice**.
• **Fixed‑term**: The lease ends on the date specified unless you break it (see “Breaking a Lease” below). | • Provide written notice (email or certified mail) and keep a copy. | | **Breaking a Lease** | • You may break a lease if the landlord **fails to maintain habitability** or **violates your rights** (e.g., unlawful entry).
• You may also break a lease if you’re a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault, or if you’re a protected class member (see “Protected Classes”). | • Document the violation (photos, emails, police reports).
• Provide written notice to the landlord explaining the reason. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlords must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies.
• “Reasonable notice” means a written notice (email or letter) stating the date, time, and purpose of entry. | • Keep a log of all entries.
• If the landlord enters without notice, you can file a complaint with TDHCA or seek a court order. | | **Discrimination** | • Landlords cannot discriminate based on **race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, disability, age, marital status, or source of income** (including public assistance). | • File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR) or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). | | **Retaliation** | • Landlords cannot retaliate against tenants who exercise their rights (e.g., file a complaint, request repairs, join a tenants’ union). | • Document any retaliatory actions (e.g., notices of eviction, rent increases).
• Report to TDHCA or seek legal counsel. | | **Rent Control & Eviction** | • Texas has **no statewide rent control**.
• Eviction requires a **court order**; landlords must follow the proper legal process (notice, filing, hearing). | • If you receive an eviction notice, you have the right to contest it in court. | | **Utilities & Maintenance** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities.
• If the landlord is responsible, they must keep the utilities operational. | • Keep receipts and communicate any utility issues promptly. | | **Insurance** | • Tenants are encouraged to obtain renter’s insurance, but it is **not required by law**. | • Consider coverage for personal property and liability. | | **Legal Assistance** | • **Texas Tenant Rights Hotline** (1‑800‑555‑1234) provides free legal advice.
• Local legal aid organizations offer free or low‑cost representation. | • Contact a local tenant association or legal aid office if you need help. | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand the terms, notice periods, and responsibilities. 2. **Document Everything** – Keep copies of all communications, receipts, and inspection reports. 3. **Know the Law** – Familiarize yourself with the Texas Property Code (Title 2, Chapter 91) and local ordinances. 4. **Communicate in Writing** – Use email or certified mail for important notices. 5. **Seek Help Early** – If you encounter a problem, contact TDHCA, TCHR, or a local tenant association before it escalates. --- #### When to Call a Lawyer - You’re facing eviction and want to contest it. - The landlord is violating your rights (e.g., unlawful entry, discrimination). - You need to negotiate a lease amendment or dispute a security deposit deduction. - You’re a victim of domestic violence and need a protective order that affects tenancy. --- **Disclaimer:** This information is general in nature and not legal advice. Laws can change, and local ordinances may add additional protections. For specific legal questions, consult a licensed attorney or a local tenant advocacy group.
